name: Abagtha
title: Eunuch at the court of King Ahasuerus
summary: Abagtha is one of seven courtiers at the Persian king's palace in Susa, mentioned with the Hebrew word 'saris', which can denote either a eunuch or a high-ranking court official. He served under King Ahasuerus, usually identified with the Persian Xerxes I. According to Esther 1:10, Abagtha was sent along with six other courtiers to bring Queen Vashti before the great banquet, so that the king could display her beauty to the guests. Vashti's refusal triggered a political crisis that led to her removal. Although Abagtha appears only briefly in the story, he is part of the sequence of events that led to Esther's elevation as queen – and thus to the deliverance of the Jewish people. In a book where God's name is never explicitly mentioned, even peripheral figures like Abagtha illustrate how seemingly ordinary actions can fit into a larger pattern of divine providence.

keyEvents.title: Service at the court of King Ahasuerus
keyEvents.description: Abagtha was one of the seven courtiers (eunuchs) who served directly under King Ahasuerus in the Persian Empire and had privileged access to the king's presence.

keyEvents.title: The order to bring Queen Vashti
keyEvents.description: On the seventh day of the king's feast, when the king was in high spirits from wine, he commanded Abagtha and the other six courtiers to bring Queen Vashti wearing her royal crown, so that her beauty might be displayed before the people and the officials.

keyEvents.title: Vashti's refusal and its consequences
keyEvents.description: When the courtiers delivered the king's command, Queen Vashti refused to come. Although Abagtha is not mentioned individually in this part of the text, he was among those sent. Her rejection led to a political crisis that ended with her removal from office, paving the way for Esther's elevation as queen.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew word 'saris' (סָרִיס), used of Abagtha, can mean both 'eunuch' and 'court official'. In the Persian Empire, it was common for eunuchs to serve in high positions at court, especially near the king's women and within the royal household.

The name Abagtha (אֲבַגְתָא) is likely of Persian origin. Some scholars link it to Old Persian 'bagadata', meaning 'given by God'. The names of the seven courtiers in Esther 1:10 are all of Persian origin, which supports the book's familiarity with Persian customs.

King Ahasuerus is commonly identified with Xerxes I (486–465 BC), who ruled over the Persian Achaemenid Empire. The great feast described in Esther 1 may be connected to Herodotus' account of Xerxes' preparations for war against Greece in 483 BC.

The Persian court had a complex hierarchy of servants and officials. The seven courtiers mentioned alongside Abagtha held a special position with direct access to the king, which in the Persian Empire was a highly privileged role. Greek sources confirm that such trusted servants were often eunuchs.

The number seven has symbolic meaning both in Persian culture and in biblical tradition. In the book of Esther, there appear seven courtiers, seven advisors, and a feast lasting seven days. According to Herodotus, in Persian tradition the number seven was associated with the seven great noble families who had special access to the king.

The book of Esther is unique in the Hebrew Bible because God's name is never explicitly mentioned. Nevertheless, Jewish and Christian interpretive tradition reads God's providence into the events—even seemingly trivial details like the naming of court officials. The fact that Abagta is named by name places him as part of the providential sequence of events leading to the salvation of the Jewish people.

The ruins of the Persian palace in Susa (biblical Shushan) have been excavated by French archaeologists since the late 19th century. The findings confirm the magnificent architecture described in the book of Esther, including the great columned hall (apadana) where the banquet likely took place.
